subject: Astronomy & Space
title: Micro Black Holes: Tiny Terrors
description: A quick, practical guide to Micro Black Holes: Tiny Terrors.

hook.text: Could black holes be smaller than an atom? Theory says yes—but none have ever been found.

buildup.text: A black hole with Earth's mass would be just 9 mm across. Shrink the mass further and it gets subatomic.

discovery.text: Some physicists hoped the Large Hadron Collider might create tiny black holes. It didn't—and that taught us something too.

twist.text: If micro black holes exist, they'd evaporate almost instantly via Hawking radiation—vanishing in a burst of energy.

climax.text: Detecting that burst would confirm Hawking radiation—one of the most important unproven predictions in physics.

punchline.text: Too small to see, too fast to catch. Proof of Hawking's greatest idea.

quiz.question: Why would micro black holes be scientifically important if detected?
options: Their evaporation would confirm Hawking radiation, a major unproven prediction
They could be used as energy sources for spacecraft
They would prove that all matter eventually becomes a black hole

details.summary: Micro black holes, hypothetically as small as subatomic particles, could have formed in the extreme conditions of the early universe. Stephen Hawking predicted they would evaporate rapidly through Hawking radiation.
details.whyItMatters: Micro black holes sit at the intersection of quantum mechanics and gravity. Detecting one — or proving they evaporate — would provide the first experimental evidence for quantum gravity.
takeaways: Hypothetical black holes as small as subatomic particles
Could have formed in the extreme early universe
Their evaporation would confirm Hawking radiation

faq.question: Could the Large Hadron Collider create micro black holes?
faq.answer: Only if extra spatial dimensions exist, which would lower the energy threshold for black hole creation. Even then, such micro black holes would evaporate in about 10^-27 seconds through Hawking radiation, posing zero danger. No evidence of their creation has been observed.

faq.question: How small can a black hole be?
faq.answer: Theoretically, the smallest meaningful black hole would have the Planck mass — about 22 micrograms — with an event horizon at the Planck length (~10^-35 meters). Below this scale, quantum effects dominate and the classical concept of a black hole breaks down entirely.
